title: Health-Zone Escalation Patterns and Early-Warning Signals During the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Retrospective Longitudinal Ecological Study
content: Introduction: National epidemic curves can conceal subnational heterogeneity after Ebola outbreak detection. This study characterised health-zone escalation patterns and early-warning signals during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Methods: A retrospective longitudinal ecological study used national situation reports through 6 September 2026 without imputation. Sixty-one affected health zones were followed across 108 reports. Five mutually exclusive escalation patterns were classified, time to ≥30 confirmed cases was analysed using Kaplan–Meier methods, and 21-day pre-transition case accumulation and spatial context were assessed using Geo-Referenced Infrastructure and Demographic Data for Development version 9.0 boundaries. Results: Of 61 health zones, 37 were classified as persistent low burden, 16 as slow escalation, three as rapid escalation, three as recurrent escalation and two as escalation after reporting silence; 22 reached ≥30 cases. Median time to transition was not reached because the probability of remaining below 30 cases stayed above 50%. The three rapid escalators were health zones named in the initial outbreak declaration and reached ≥30 cases within 9–11 days of first confirmed attribution. Eighteen of 19 rapid or slow escalation zones accumulated more cases during the 21 days before reaching ≥30 cumulative confirmed cases than at least 75% of persistent low zones followed for the same duration; one matched the 75th-percentile value. All 16 slow-escalation zones had an active adjacent zone and 13 a high-burden adjacent zone; among rapid zones, two of three had an active adjacent zone and none a high-burden zone. Neighbouring-zone differences were descriptive and were not evaluated as predictors. Conclusion: Distinct escalation patterns support differentiated subnational surveillance. Rapid within-zone increases warrant immediate verification, whereas neighbouring-zone activity may help prioritise review of slower escalation. Recurrence after a quiet interval and apparent escalation after reporting silence represent distinct surveillance states requiring different verification and response pathways.
